title: Defining the Boundary of What Is Impossible Relative to the Sum of All Quantum Events and Other Domains
content: This paper proposes an evidence-based definition for what is “statistically impossible” relative to an appropriate set of domains, including the universe of all quantum events, all possible earthly events, the history of all human events, and a human lifetime.  For example, any event which has less than one chance of occurring in the total number of all quantum vibrations in the history of the universe (10120) should, according to this proposed convention, be confidently declared as “statistically impossible.”  Moreover, sequences of events that are less likely than the square of all quantum events in the universe (10240) (which is equal to all quantum events in 10120 multiverses) are properly described as “absurdly impossible.”According to this convention, if such a "statistically impossible" event is ever observed then one must conclude either: (A) the observed event is non-random, or (B) the universe of all possible events is larger than previously assumed.  This convention is therefore useful for testing a priori assumptions and distinguishing random from non-random events.  Also discussed is the need for a new ratio, similar to an effect size calculation, for describing the likelihood of a series of events within a given domain of possible events as either “certain”, “likely”, “possible”, “improbable”, and “impossible.”
